text: search in 500 words without using tools.

content.text:
search is an algorithm for finding a target value in a sorted collection by repeatedly cutting the remaining search space in half. Instead of scanning every element, it asks a yes-or-no question about the middle: is the target smaller, equal, or larger? Each answer discards half of what is left, so the number of comparisons grows with the logarithm of the input size.

The setup is simple. You have a sequence already ordered, usually in nondecreasing order, and an indexable structure such as an array. You keep two bounds: a low index at the start of the remaining range and a high index at the end. While low is not past high, you compute a midpoint. If the value at the midpoint is the target, you are done. If the midpoint is too small, the target—if it exists—must lie to the right, so you raise low just past the midpoint. If the midpoint is too large, you lower high just before it. When the range collapses without a match, the target is absent.

That halving is why the complexity is O(log n). An array of a million items needs only about twenty comparisons in the worst case, because 2^20 is a little over a million. Linear search would need up to a million comparisons. The price of that speed is the ordering requirement: without a total order you can trust, the midpoint comparison does not tell you which half to throw away.

Implementation details matter. Integer overflow in the midpoint formula is a classic bug: `(low + high) / 2` can overflow in languages with fixed-width integers, so `low + (high - low) / 2` is safer. Duplicate values raise a policy question: do you want any match, the leftmost, or the rightmost? Finding insertion points is the same loop with a different exit: lower bound is the first index not less than the target; upper bound is the first index strictly greater. Those variants turn search into a building block for counting, ranking, and range queries.

Binary search also appears outside arrays. On a monotonic predicate over integers, you can search the domain of a function: the first true, the last false, the smallest feasible capacity, the earliest timestamp that satisfies a condition. The same idea applies to floating-point ranges until the interval is small enough. In trees, a binary search tree stores the order in the shape of the data so each comparison still discards a subtree, though balance determines whether that subtree is truly about half.

The algorithm is not magic. It fails on unsorted data, on comparisons that are inconsistent, and on floating-point noise that breaks monotonicity. It also has a small constant-factor disadvantage on tiny arrays, where a linear scan can be faster because of simpler control flow and better cache behavior. For large sorted data, though, it is one of the most reliable tools in programming: few lines of code, a clear invariant, and a guarantee that each step really does reduce the problem by half. That combination—sorted input, midpoint test, shrinking interval—is the whole method.
